quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Who' introduces extra information about the manager, right in the middle of the sentence.
quests.explanation: Subject (The manager) + relative clause (who hired me) + verb (just resigned). The relative clause sits between the subject and its main verb, describing 'the manager'.
quests.textToSpeak: The manager who hired me just resigned.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'That' links back to 'the book', introducing a clause describing which one.
quests.explanation: Subject (I) + verb (found) + object (the book) + relative clause (that you recommended). 'That' can replace 'which' when describing things, especially in speech.
quests.textToSpeak: I found the book that you recommended.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: The whole subject, including its relative clause, comes before the main verb 'is'.
quests.explanation: Subject (The company which won the contract) + verb (is) + adjective (local). The relative clause 'which won the contract' identifies exactly which company.
quests.textToSpeak: The company which won the contract is local.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: No relative pronoun appears here at all — 'she bought last month' attaches directly to 'car'.
quests.explanation: Subject (The car) + relative clause (she bought last month, pronoun omitted) + verb (broke down). When the relative pronoun is the object, it can often be left out.
quests.textToSpeak: The car she bought last month broke down.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Whom' is set off by commas here, adding extra detail without changing who is meant.
quests.explanation: Subject (My colleague) + relative clause ('whom I mentioned earlier', extra information) + verb (just walked in). Commas signal that the clause simply adds detail, not identifying information.
quests.textToSpeak: My colleague, whom I mentioned earlier, just walked in.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: Again, no relative pronoun appears — 'we discussed yesterday' sits right after 'plan'.
quests.explanation: Subject (The plan) + relative clause (we discussed yesterday, pronoun omitted) + verb (needs revising). Omitting the object relative pronoun is very common in natural spoken English.
quests.textToSpeak: The plan we discussed yesterday needs revising.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Whose' shows possession inside the clause — the essay belongs to the student.
quests.explanation: Subject (The student) + relative clause (whose essay won) + verb (lives) + place (nearby). 'Whose' introduces a clause showing that something belongs to the subject.
quests.textToSpeak: The student whose essay won lives nearby.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Where' introduces a clause describing a place, standing in for 'in which'.
quests.explanation: Subject (This) + verb (is) + object (the office) + relative clause (where I used to work). 'Where' replaces a longer phrase like 'in which' when describing a place.
quests.textToSpeak: This is the office where I used to work.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Whose dog barked' explains why the man apologized, tucked inside the subject.
quests.explanation: Subject (A man) + relative clause (whose dog barked) + verb (apologized) + adverb (quickly). The relative clause explains the reason for the action that follows.
quests.textToSpeak: A man whose dog barked apologized quickly.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: The doer of the action isn't mentioned — only what happens to the reports matters here.
quests.explanation: Subject (Reports) + 'are' + past participle (reviewed) + time (every Friday). Passive voice focuses on the action's receiver when the doer isn't important.
quests.textToSpeak: Reports are reviewed every Friday.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'By most companies' names who performs the action, added at the very end.
quests.explanation: Subject (This software) + 'is' + past participle (used) + 'by most companies'. 'By' introduces the agent when the passive sentence chooses to mention it.
quests.textToSpeak: This software is used by most companies.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Are trained' shows the passive form matches the plural subject.
quests.explanation: Subject (New employees) + 'are' + past participle (trained) + time ('during their first week'). Passive verbs must agree in number with their subject, just like active ones.
quests.textToSpeak: New employees are trained during their first week.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Was built' places the construction firmly in the past, with no builder named.
quests.explanation: Subject (This bridge) + 'was' + past participle (built) + time ('in the 1960s'). Past passive uses 'was' or 'were' plus the past participle.
quests.textToSpeak: This bridge was built in the 1960s.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Without much discussion' describes how the decision happened, closing the sentence.
quests.explanation: Subject (That decision) + 'was' + past participle (made) + manner ('without much discussion'). The passive here avoids naming exactly who made the decision.
quests.textToSpeak: That decision was made without much discussion.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Were' matches the plural subject 'errors', not the singular 'draft' that follows.
quests.explanation: Subject (Several errors) + 'were' + past participle (found) + place ('in the final draft'). The passive verb agrees with 'errors', the true subject of the sentence.
quests.textToSpeak: Several errors were found in the final draft.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: The 'if' clause uses past tense, even though it's talking about an unreal present situation.
quests.explanation: 'If' + unreal condition (I had more time, past form) + result (I would travel more). Second conditional uses past tense in the 'if' clause to show it isn't real.
quests.textToSpeak: If I had more time, I would travel more.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: The result leads this time, with the unreal condition trailing after 'if'.
quests.explanation: Result (She would accept the offer) + 'if' + unreal condition (it paid better, past form). 'Would' plus a past-tense 'if' clause describes an imagined, unlikely situation.
quests.textToSpeak: She would accept the offer if it paid better.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'We'd' contracts 'we would' smoothly into the result clause.
quests.explanation: 'If' + unreal condition (we lived closer) + result ('we'd see each other often', would + base). Second conditional imagines a different, currently untrue situation.
quests.textToSpeak: If we lived closer, we'd see each other often.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: This is a question form of the second conditional — 'would' fronts the sentence before the subject.
quests.explanation: 'What' + 'would' + subject (you) + base verb (do) + 'if' + unreal condition (you lost your job)? Second conditional questions invert 'would' and the subject, just like other modal questions.
quests.textToSpeak: What would you do if you lost your job?

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Were', not 'was', is used here even with 'I' — a special rule for this exact expression.
quests.explanation: Subject (I) + 'wouldn't' + verb (worry) + 'if I were you'. 'If I were you' always uses 'were', even though 'I' is singular — this is a fixed expression for giving advice.
quests.textToSpeak: I wouldn't worry if I were you.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Might' replaces 'would' here, showing the result is only a weaker possibility.
quests.explanation: 'If' + unreal condition (he asked nicely) + result (she might reconsider). 'Might' instead of 'would' shows a less certain possible outcome.
quests.textToSpeak: If he asked nicely, she might reconsider.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: The tense shifts back one step: 'parked' becomes 'had parked' in the reported version.
quests.explanation: Subject (He) + verb (asked) + 'where' + reported clause (I had parked the car, shifted back). Reported speech often pushes the original tense one step further into the past.
quests.textToSpeak: He asked where I had parked the car.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Whether' works like 'if' here, introducing a reported yes/no question.
quests.explanation: Subject (She) + verb (wondered) + 'whether' + reported clause (the offer was still open). 'Whether' is a slightly more formal alternative to 'if' in reported questions.
quests.textToSpeak: She wondered whether the offer was still open.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Will' shifts to 'would' in the reported version, matching the reported-speech pattern.
quests.explanation: Subject (They) + 'wanted to know' + 'when' + reported clause (the results would arrive, will shifted to would). Future 'will' becomes 'would' when reported from a past point of view.
quests.textToSpeak: They wanted to know when the results would arrive.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Rarely' takes the same mid-sentence spot other frequency adverbs use, before the main verb.
quests.explanation: Subject (I) + frequency (rarely) + verb (eat out) + time ('during the week'). Frequency adverbs like 'rarely' sit between the subject and the main verb.
quests.textToSpeak: I rarely eat out during the week.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Completely' slides between the auxiliary and the past participle, intensifying the verb.
quests.explanation: Subject (She) + 'had' + adverb (completely) + past participle (forgotten) + 'about the appointment'. Degree adverbs like 'completely' often sit inside a perfect verb phrase.
quests.textToSpeak: She had completely forgotten about the appointment.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Probably' also slots inside the verb phrase, expressing likelihood rather than certainty.
quests.explanation: 'We've' + adverb (probably) + past participle (missed) + object (the last train) + 'by now'. Adverbs of probability commonly appear right after the auxiliary in a perfect tense.
quests.textToSpeak: We've probably missed the last train by now.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: A relative clause and a passive verb combine inside the very first noun phrase.
quests.explanation: Subject (A proposal that was rejected last year, containing a passive relative clause) + verb (might get approved) + time (now). Relative clauses can themselves contain a passive verb.
quests.textToSpeak: A proposal that was rejected last year might get approved now.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: A relative clause is tucked inside the 'if' condition, before the unreal result follows.
quests.explanation: 'If' + unreal condition (the manager who hired me were still here, containing a relative clause) + result (things would be different). Second conditional clauses can carry their own relative clause.
quests.textToSpeak: If the manager who hired me were still here, things would be different.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: A place-relative clause sits inside the subject, and the whole thing takes a passive verb.
quests.explanation: Subject (The house where we grew up, containing a relative clause) + 'was' + past participle (sold) + time ('last spring'). A relative clause and a passive verb can combine naturally in one sentence.
quests.textToSpeak: The house where we grew up was sold last spring.
